repos.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
repos.paper_summary: Harness2 is a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing. It refines an LLM agent's execution harness (its prompts, memory, skills, tools, and related components) for each task, and it updates a separate improvement harness across tasks. Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step. It proposes harness edits, runs them under matched conditions against a reference execution, and composes only changes supported by behavioral contrasts, without a ground-truth verifier. Parallel recursion composes from a pool of candidates, and sequential recursion chains revisions. Both are controlled by a budget k. After each task, reflection adds adopted harnesses and supported lessons to a library that guides later proposals. On WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB (Partial pass rate), with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex, one step improves every configuration by up to 11.5 points, 4.5 points, and 11.8 percentage points. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds up to 3.9, 4.2, and 6.7 more. The authors state that probe contrasts are limited by execution stochasticity and shared model biases, and that adopted harnesses are not verified to be optimal.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 targets open-world agent harness evolution, which lacks ground-truth verifiers and fails to transfer across tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness2
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 pairs task-level recursion, which refines the current harness without verifiers, with a library that carries lessons to later tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-step Harness2 exceeds the base harness on all three benchmarks for GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under both initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Score gains grow with recursion budget, and each ablated component lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 differs from prior harness optimization by learning from its own refinements across a task stream without ground-truth feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 turns task-specific refinement into reusable experience, with gains reported across three benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers comparison criteria, benchmark splits, baselines, tool-call errors, production harness comparison, failure cases, limitations, and prompts.

repos.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
DuoLM is a framework for personalized recommendation that pairs a compact item encoder and personalized ranker with a serving runtime that reuses computation. An encoder LLM maps each item's text to one vector computed offline. A ranker LLM takes these vectors in place of item text, plus user history and feedback, and scores candidates with a linear head. Both models are trained jointly with cross-entropy on observed targets and KL distillation from a frozen full-text teacher. The runtime resolves virtual token IDs to stored vectors, prefills each request's history once, and scores candidates in independent branches on SGLang, with CUDA Graph replay.

On Amazon Books, next-item NDCG@10 is 0.5586 versus 0.5440 for the teacher. On Video Games it is 0.5298 versus 0.5313. On one H100, the system scores about 26,400 candidates per second, which the paper reports as 60.1× the teacher served with vLLM. Limitations: evaluation covers two Amazon datasets with 0.6B backbones and fixed candidate sets with random negatives; one vector per item may drop user-specific detail; and throughput excludes training and offline encoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Language-model recommenders must cut online computation and serving overhead, and DuoLM addresses both with compact reusable item vectors and a serving runtime.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: An encoder turns each item into one reusable vector, a ranker scores candidates from history vectors, and serving shares history computation across candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment Settings
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use 0.6B Qwen3 backbones on Amazon Books and Video Games against a full-text teacher and other baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: DuoLM stays close to the full-text teacher in quality and serves up to 26,403.98 candidate scores per second on one H100.

repos.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
repos.paper_summary: AIPOCH Open-Science is an open-source AI research workbench that exports and imports research sessions as portable `.science` packages. The package keeps recorded relations among task context, executed activities, artifact versions, reviews and retained files, and it maps identifiers to the receiving workspace. The authors specify this exchange contract and test it on one controlled session with an incorrect first output, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted permutation test. Complete and partial exports were compared with source snapshots extracted independently of the exporter, and both imports into separate projects retained the tested version and review associations. The unreviewed revision stayed distinct from earlier assessments, and excluded content was marked unavailable. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution and review. Offline re-execution of its retained script on a fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. Limitations stated by the paper include that the controlled test used one session and one installation, that native input-edge rows were absent, and that initial task attribution still depends on the surrounding conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Author affiliations
digest_headlines.headline: The author list spans many hospitals and companies, mainly in China, with affiliations also in the Netherlands, Israel and the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sharing AI-assisted research needs its task, version and review relations to survive transfer, not only the output files.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier provenance and session-sharing systems cover parts of the problem; this work focuses on version and review attribution after exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods and implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The method maps workbench records into typed objects and relations, then checks an exported package against an independently extracted source reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Relations, not just files, survived export in a controlled session, with all paired comparisons matching in both exchange conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A failed assessment, its correction and an unreviewed revision can all be true together, so exchange must keep each target separate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The contract keeps recorded version and review relations across identifier mapping and explicit omissions, with evidence limited to the tested records.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The software is released under Apache 2.0, and a de-identified validation release on Hugging Face contains the protocol, packages and audit scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Codex assisted with literature retrieval, source inspection, application operation and validation code, and the authors remain responsible for interpretation.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplementary figure lists case16 evidence associations and an offline re-execution that reproduced two saved tables byte for byte.

repos.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
repos.paper_summary: TokenEconomizer is an external controller that reduces token costs for black-box coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI) over sequences of tasks within the same repository, without modifying model weights or agent code. It applies three meta-strategies whose policies are learned from completed traces: activating repository-specific micro-skills, pruning loaded tools that are never called, and intervening in failure loops using a turn budget set from successful prior runs, with an LLM judge deciding whether to redirect or stop. Evaluation covers 277 SWE-Bench tasks across six repositories in five agent–model settings, plus 102 Web-Bench tasks and 200 security-auditing tasks. On SWE-Bench, mean cache-aware cost falls by 18.4–30.9% including controller overhead, and Pass@1 rises in four of five settings; the one drop is 1.0 percentage point on Opus 4.8. Reduced reasoning effort lowers Pass@1 by 1.8–10.3 points in comparison. On Web-Bench and the security benchmarks, cost falls by 16.0–21.2% and 6.4–19.6%, with Pass@2 and detection F1 comparable to default. Limitations: the controller can make incorrect decisions (stale skills, wrongly pruned tools, mistaken loop detection), and SWE-Bench task streams are independent fixes rather than real user sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Recurring coding-agent costs in shared repositories motivate an external controller that learns from completed tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Cost Profiling and Analysis of Fixed Cost-control Strategies
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed cost-control strategies give mixed results by repository, and traces reveal three sources of removable cost.

digest_headlines.heading: TokenEconomizer
digest_headlines.headline: TokenEconomizer selects micro-skills, tool masks, and turn budgets per repository using confirmation, retirement, and failure-loop rules learned from traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the software-engineering benchmark, TokenEconomizer cuts mean cost 18.4–30.9% across five settings, raising Pass@1 in four.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing agent cost methods are typically fixed and task-local, whereas TokenEconomizer adapts cost control from completed traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stale skills, wrongly pruned tools, and mistaken loop detections remain possible, and streams are not real user sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers extended discussion, cost-profiling protocol, controller configuration, task selection, examples, and harness customization.

repos.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
repos.paper_summary:
Matrix-Game 4.0 is a real-time game-world system that separates game execution from visual generation. A lightweight engine keeps world state and enforces rules, a coding agent turns player requests into game code and captions, and an autoregressive video renderer turns low-poly proxy frames into detailed 480p frames.

The renderer adapts Wan2.2 5B to video-to-video generation. It is conditioned on the proxy, a per-frame caption built from engine state, reference frames, and the first frame. It is trained on 114,334 paired UE5 clips (1,712 hours), then distilled into a causal generator that produces four-frame chunks in one or two denoising steps.

On one RTX 5090 at 480p, the paper reports 60 FPS gameplay, 112 ms key-press-to-display latency, and 83 FPS single-step steady-state throughput with 18.2 GiB peak memory. Against the unoptimized causal baseline (4.5 FPS, 1110 ms), the cumulative optimizations give 19× throughput and 9.9× lower latency. The latency figure applies only to the evaluated configuration. The authors list lower inference cost, visual fidelity, higher-resolution refinement, and multiplayer rendering as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Playable worlds need persistent state, executable rules and low latency, which motivates separating game logic from video generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Roadmap
digest_headlines.headline: A game engine, a coding agent and a video model form a harness, with the engine holding world state and enforcing rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Paired Unreal Engine captures of low-poly and high-fidelity video give 114,334 training clips across four scene types.

digest_headlines.heading: Rendering Model
digest_headlines.headline: A video model is distilled into a causal generator that denoises each four-frame chunk in one or two steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-Time Inference
digest_headlines.headline: Cumulative optimizations raise steady-state throughput from 4.5 to 83.4 FPS and cut latency from 1110 ms to 112 ms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Visual results are qualitative only, but Matrix-Game 4.0 reports the lowest latency among four compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior interactive models keep dynamics in the network, while several recent systems assign rules to code and render with video.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The harness design is offered as a reusable foundation, with lower inference cost and hardware needs left as near-term work.

repos.title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
repos.paper_summary:
nanoflann is a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact nearest-neighbor search on product manifolds declared at compile time, such as SO(2), SO(3), S^n, SE(2), SE(3), and tori. The distance is a weighted squared product metric. Circular coordinates use wrapped distance, and SO(3) uses the chordal distance on unit quaternions, taking a minimum over the antipodal cover. Pruning uses a per-coordinate lower bound that the paper proves admissible, so a pruned subtree cannot contain a closer neighbor. The paper also adds an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for frequent insertions and deletions, such as sliding-window LiDAR maps.

Reported results: exact search gives recall 1.0 against an exhaustive scan under the same metric, while Euclidean search on raw coordinates drops to about 0.5^m for m rotation blocks. The method reaches up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. The incremental index has lower update latency than the ikd-Tree. The provided text ends before the full experimental tables, so dataset details and the size of that gain are not given.

Limitations: unit-norm quaternions are assumed when chordal distance is read as a rotation angle, and angles must be normalized to [−π, π].

digest_headlines.heading: INTRODUCTION
digest_headlines.headline: Exact nearest-neighbor search on non-Euclidean robotics spaces needs a general, dependency-free KD-tree rather than planning-specific libraries.

digest_headlines.heading: RELATED WORK
digest_headlines.headline: Prior exact manifold KD-trees hard-code their space sets and store per-node topological state, which this work avoids.

digest_headlines.heading: BACKGROUND: EUCLIDEAN KD-TREE
digest_headlines.headline: A Euclidean KD-tree prunes with a per-dimension squared gap to the split value, and generalizing that term is the core contribution.

digest_headlines.heading: EXACT NN ON PRODUCT MANIFOLDS
digest_headlines.headline: A coordinate-wise admissible bound, wrap-aware for circles and double-cover-aware for quaternions, makes pruning exact on product manifolds.

digest_headlines.heading: INCREMENTAL SELF-BALANCING INDEX
digest_headlines.headline: An incremental single tree with lazy deletes and pooled memory supports changing point sets, with an optional asynchronous rebuild mode.

digest_headlines.heading: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
digest_headlines.headline: Exact search returns recall 1.0 against brute force, while a Euclidean tree on raw coordinates drops to 0.26 with two quaternion blocks.

digest_headlines.heading: CONCLUSIONS
digest_headlines.headline: The library gives exact product-manifold search with no per-node storage, and its incremental index beats ikd-Tree on update latency.

repos.title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
repos.paper_summary: MOSS-Image is an open-weight text-to-image system built from a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) pretrained from scratch and an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancer that turns short requests into content and layout specifications. The DiT takes text features from a frozen Qwen3.5-9B encoder and latents from a frozen FLUX.2 VAE, and uses 4D RoPE, SiTU-GLU feed-forward layers, and a hybrid Muon–AdamW optimizer. Pretraining uses about 3 billion images after deduplication and AI-image removal, with multi-granularity recaptions, bounding-box JSON annotations, and three resolution stages. The authors introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB), with 240 English and Chinese literary-text tasks, and RealLayoutArena (RLA), with 61 design requests scored by blind pairwise human comparison on an Elo scale. On LLTB, MOSS-Image scores 96.3 Mean-6, the highest among the open-weight models listed. On 7Bench, it reaches 0.88 `mIoU_det` and 0.70 Layout AUC, versus 0.44 and 0.20 for Ideogram 4. On RLA, it ranks second at 1698.70 Elo, behind GPT Image 2 at 1844.35. Under shared enhanced prompts, its backbone ranks first at 1807.34 Elo. Stated limitations: no reference-image conditioning or editing, and the enhancer depends on external language models.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Open-weight models struggle with dense text, so MOSS-Image pairs a 5B diffusion transformer with an agentic prompt enhancer.

digest_headlines.heading: System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: The system pairs a pretrained text-and-layout renderer with an enhancer that turns concise requests into specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Pretraining Strategy
digest_headlines.headline: A 5B DiT pretrained from scratch on 3 billion deduplicated images keeps broad data and uses multi-granularity captions.

digest_headlines.heading: Agentic Prompt Enhancement
digest_headlines.headline: An agent routes each request to task guidance and writes structured layouts with literal text, bounding boxes and typography.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On LLTB, MOSS-Image scores 96.3 Mean-6, and on RLA it ranks second end-to-end at 1698.70 Elo.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study
digest_headlines.headline: Qualitative cases report that layout prompts enable zero-shot edits, line breaks help text rendering, and zero-centered boxes transfer to unseen resolutions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers foundation models, visual text generation, layout conditioning, prompt agents and text-rich evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The backbone cannot condition on reference images or edit images, and the enhancer's errors can reduce specification quality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A capable renderer combined with explicit generation specifications supports complex graphics, according to the LLTB and RLA results.

digest_headlines.heading: Contributors
digest_headlines.headline: The contributor list names the project leads, core contributors, other contributors and advisors.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the architecture, training, dataset, filtering, figure and related-work details behind the main text.

repos.title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
repos.paper_summary: cuRoboV2-Fast is a GPU-accelerated motion planner for collision-free, torque-limited robot motions that reduces planning latency and execution time. It combines a bounded bidirectional RRT for route initialization, B-spline trajectory optimization with parallel evaluation and gradient gathering, TimeOpt (a solver that retimes a fixed path under velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds), and differentiable inverse dynamics that accept payload changes without recompiling. On 2,575 MotionBenchMaker and MPINets queries, its RRT reaches 98.68% initialization success at 0.305 ms mean planning time, versus 91.92% for cuRoboV1 PRM and 88.27% for cuRoboV2 PRM. With a 3 kg payload on an RTX 5090, mean planning time is 4.43 ms, 14.7× faster than cuRoboV2. TimeOpt cuts mean motion time by 15.7% relative to the refined trajectory. Success stays near cuRoboV2 across payloads and exceeds the TOPPRA baselines by 14.5–15.7 percentage points at the heaviest payload. TimeOpt finds a local minimum and does not guarantee global optimality. Its advantage is shown on Franka Panda and YAM setups.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Planning time and execution time both matter, and cuRoboV2-Fast targets both for payload-aware, torque-limited motions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers parallel planners, B-spline refinement, and fixed-path timing, and the method builds on each.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: The planner fits B-spline trajectories to a parallel tree-search seed, then retimes them with TimeOpt under payload-dependent torque limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show lower planning and motion times than cuRoboV2 at similar success, with real-robot gains in arm execution time.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Fewer iterations, cheaper iterations, and TimeOpt timing drive the gains, while planning is only 1.0% of real-robot cycle time.

repos.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
repos.paper_summary: StartLux-Decision is a family of 0.8B–27B decision models that output probability distributions over candidate options for typed questions. The Instant variant makes one forward pass with bidirectional attention in its full-attention layers. The AutoThink variant first makes a one-pass prediction, then generates a reasoning trace of up to 4,096 tokens only when its top probability is below 0.9, and averages the initial and post-reasoning distributions. The final training stage adds reasoning supervision and RLCD2, which uses a frozen reference model, proper-score rewards, and a soft length penalty. RLCD2 raises the share of traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, with accuracy largely preserved. On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models beat the strongest comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink reaches 73.4. On DecisionPivot, a programmatically generated benchmark of contrast pairs, AutoThink beats its Instant counterpart by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy. Policy-aware calibration reduces confidence–accuracy gaps to within 2.7 points across 184 settings. Stated limitations include generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift, both left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models need reasoning on hard cases without losing single-pass efficiency; the paper proposes two variants, RLCD2 training, and DecisionPivot.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design and Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage training gives Instant bidirectional attention and teaches AutoThink to reason only when its confidence is below 0.9.

digest_headlines.heading: RLCD2: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: RLCD2 rewards reasoning by the change in proper score and penalizes traces beyond a soft budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models lead comparable-scale references by 7.4–16.9 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Capability and Reliability Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Selecting among candidates makes reported confidence overconfident, and policy-aware calibration narrows the gaps across 184 settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Inference and Deployment
digest_headlines.headline: Single-pass Instant readouts on a single GPU take 24–52 ms for 256-token prompts and 31–98 ms for 1,024-token prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix documents training data sources and decontamination, policy-aware calibration proofs, and serving configuration safeguards.

repos.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
repos.paper_summary: WeVisOne-VL is a vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL at 2B and 4B scales. It unifies object-level and pixel-level perception in one structured next-token output. Supported tasks include detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, referring segmentation, and image matting. Coordinates are emitted as dedicated tokens for values from 0 to 1000. After each predicted box, the model emits a special OBJ token. Its hidden state, the box, and multi-level ViT features feed a lightweight pixel decoder of about 9.6M parameters that predicts a mask or alpha matte. Training is three-stage SFT followed by GRPO-based mixed-task RL on samples where the SFT model is most uncertain. The data engine covers about 100M images and 3.6B box annotations, using detector proposals verified by a VLM and hard negatives for absent targets. The paper reports leading results across over 30 benchmarks, but the provided text gives no numeric scores. Stated limitations: limited general-purpose training data may reduce general capability, outputs are produced without chain-of-thought, and inference is single-turn.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current vision-language models are unreliable for fine-grained perception, so this report proposes one model covering object-level and pixel-level tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
digest_headlines.headline: The data engine yields over 100 million images and approximately 3.6 billion bounding-box annotations, with verification and error-driven refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design
digest_headlines.headline: The model writes tasks as text with coordinate tokens and adds a lightweight decoder that turns object tokens into full-resolution masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses three supervised fine-tuning stages, then reinforcement learning on uncertainty-selected samples with box-based grounding rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: WeVisOne-VL-4B reaches 57.1 mean F1 on COCO and 71.3 on Dense200, above the comparable VLMs listed.

digest_headlines.heading: Qualitative Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Qualitative examples show finer instance separation, correct rejection of absent targets, and cleaner matte boundaries than the baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places the model among open-vocabulary detectors, grounded multimodal models, referring segmentation systems and promptable matting methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include possible loss of general capability, no chain-of-thought reasoning, single-turn prediction, and unclear user intent.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The model improves detection F1 and counting over comparable VLMs and surpasses the evaluated baselines on referring segmentation and matting.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training corpus sources and counts, along with hyperparameters, pixel decoder training settings and RL reward definitions.
